original_draft: The Moon is not Earth's only natural satellite. Its average distance from Earth is about 768,800 kilometres, and its diameter is roughly 3,474 kilometres, a little more than a quarter of Earth's. The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth relative to the stars. Because its rotation is synchronised with its orbit, the same face always points toward Earth. On July 20, 1968, the Apollo 11 lunar module landed in the Sea of Tranquility, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the lunar surface. Buzz Aldrin joined him shortly afterwards, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia.
final_answer: The Moon is the only natural satellite of Earth. Its average distance from Earth is about 384,400 kilometres, and its diameter is roughly 3,474 kilometres, a little more than a quarter of Earth's. The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth relative to the stars. Because its rotation is synchronised with its orbit, the same face always points toward Earth. On July 20, 1969, the Apollo 11 lunar module landed in the Sea of Tranquility, and Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the lunar surface. Buzz Aldrin joined him shortly afterwards, while Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia.
